# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

screens.why5: The box took my two benefits as I typed them, "Hours back at the end of the day" and "Action items to the crew the same day", without rewording them.
screens.why7: The screen asks for what the card says it should: one to four benefits of up to nine words each, one a row, against today's way, with I'm not sure as the founder's escape; my two rows fit, and any trimming of the crew one against the log hard case belongs to the Check.

screens.why1: Right after I said what Fresco does better, Keel shows my benefits back as rows to check, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Both rows are in a super's own words: hours back at the end of the day, and action items to the crew the same day.
screens.why3: Both are things I know from my own supes: the hours in the trailer after the walk, and getting the crew their items before tomorrow.
screens.why4: Two distinct rows, each under nine words, one gain per row, no overlap; they match what I'd lead with (time back, and texting the crew).
screens.why5: It keeps my 'during the site walks, not after' and '90% faster' as time back, and my texting the crew as same-day action items, with no number I didn't write.
screens.why7: Both benefits are carried in order and joined with 'and', but the belief hangs them on 'their last daily log', a plain last occasion, not the moment the log went wrong (the study's hard case), so a super whose last log went fine would rightly answer No difference.
screens.instead: Keep both rows; have Keel test: For most, with it, their last daily log that ran into the evening after the walk would have given them hours back at the end of the day and action items to the crew the same day.

screens.why1: Right after what it does better, asking what my supers have to take on to start using it is the obvious next question before the study gets to price and buying.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps, learning, up to four, nine words each: plain to me, and my two rows are in a super's own words (who owns each item, check the notes before they go out).
screens.why3: I know exactly what a super has to do differently on the walk and before the notes go to the crew and Procore, so I can answer this from my own product and my customers.
screens.why4: The box takes my rows as I typed them, and the single 'I'm not sure' chip is the right way out for a founder who cannot name the effort.
screens.why5: Both rows are mine as typed, the walk's owner-naming and the review before sending, with nothing reworded or added.
screens.why7: Two efforts within the 1 to 4, each a base-form verb phrase of at most nine words in the third person, each a step the super takes themselves (not a sign-off, not Procore fit, not the purchase), and the founder's escape 'I'm not sure' is present as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, Keel hands back the list of efforts for me to check, which is exactly where it belongs in the solution step.
screens.why2: Naming who owns each item and checking the notes before they go out to the crew or Procore are how a super talks about punch items and logs, so I read both on first pass.
screens.why3: Both are things a super does with their own hands on the walk and in the trailer, which they can answer from their own week.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one a habit on the walk and one a review before sending, with no overlap and nothing silly.
screens.why5: These are my mechanism's real asks, assignees spoken into the video and a super who signs their own log checking what Fresco wrote, without drifting from my pitch.
screens.why7: Each row is a base-form step the super takes themselves, in the 'their' voice and under 9 words, and none repeats Compatibility's filming over the noise or Purchase friction's Procore check, so either pick gives a belief that Yes or No can answer.

screens.why1: Right after I wrote and checked the efforts, I pick the one to test; that is the natural next step and nothing here was asked before.
screens.why2: "Name who owns each item as they film" and "Check and fix the notes before they go out" are how a super talks about punch items and the log, so I read them at once.
screens.why3: Both are things a super does on the walk or in the trailer, so a super can say from their own day whether they'd do them.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, both mine and in my words: one is a new habit on the walk, the other a check before the notes go out, with no overlap and nothing missing from what I typed.
screens.why5: My narrated example "needs replacement by Alex" is exactly naming the owner as you film, and the list and belief keep it without rewording.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form steps the super takes themselves, in their voice, two within 1 to 4, neither repeating Compatibility (filming or talking over the noise) or Purchase friction; the belief can be held or refuted on the yes/only-if versus probably-not/no split, with the bar and the item's I can't tell as the card sets.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether to collect emails from supers who'd try Fresco on a live job, which is what I want from launch.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with 'Yes, ask them / No pilot' and a hint quoting the exact line respondents will see reads at a glance to me as the founder.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot sign-ups is my own call about my own launch, nothing I'd have to guess at.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice here, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: It keeps my intent: I sell per site and want people to try it on a real job, and the line respondents see names no product or role.
screens.instead: Keep the question, but have the hint say whether the email line goes to superintendents, contractor operations leads, or both, since my buyer is the contractor and a super can't start a site pilot alone.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs here, after the pilot offer and just before the link goes out to supers, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, typed answers, credits and recording into one dense paragraph, and it says 'voice' while the pick is recorded as a 'face', so I'd read it twice to know what I'm locking.
screens.why3: I can play both five-second clips and judge which one a super would listen to in the trailer or on site.
screens.why4: Two distinct interviewers, each with a preview, the default marked and the cost the same either way; no escape is needed for a pick like this.
screens.why5: Nothing of Fresco's product, price or roles is touched; it only says Keel will ask construction superintendents by text-message link.
screens.instead: Who should ask construction superintendents your questions? (Daphne, picked for you / Saskia; both play a 5 s sample; same 400 credits either way)

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, picking how superintendents answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: The three options are short and plain, and 'Daphne' is explained right in the option text, so I read it once and know what each means.
screens.why3: I know my supes are on their phones in the truck or trailer and whether they'd rather tap through or talk to a video, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: AI video, read-and-tap, and let-them-choose cover the real choices without overlap, and 'Read and tap' with speak-or-type in the boxes fits a super with gloves off at the end of the day.
screens.why5: Nothing about Fresco's product, the CFO, or the contractor buyer leaks here; it only asks how the interview reaches superintendents.

screens.why1: After choosing how superintendents answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three options are plain English. 'Contacts page' and 'signs in with Google' are self-explanatory to a founder setting up a send.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to supers I've met on job sites, to a list, or posting in a group, so this is answerable from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list, and one open link in a group are distinct and cover the realistic ways I'd reach supers; no escape is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: The screen carries no product, role or study wording that could drift or leak; it is about distribution only.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is plain and '3 counted · 5 needed' sits on each card, but the headline ties it to Compatibility alone, though all three cards are equally short, so I can't see why that one card decides it.
screens.why_b2: The stage page has no chart; the tally '3 beliefs: 3 too few to call · 7 people answered' and the per-card '3 counted · 5 needed' give the count and the bar, but the gap between 7 answered and 3 counted takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are mine and the beliefs are recognisable, but the statement under the title repeats itself ('turns them into notes with photos, assignees and due dates ... and gets back notes with photos, assignees and due dates'), and the Relative advantage line is reworded clumsily.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next: it doesn't tell me why four of seven supers weren't counted or that I need at least two more counted answers per belief before this can be called.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered: n=7 and 3 counted are on every line, and it refuses to call a result on 3 of 5 needed.
screens.instead: Too few to call on any of the three: 3 of 7 supers counted on each (the other 4 weren't asked these questions or said they hadn't walked a site) and 5 are needed, so send the study to at least 4 more superintendents who walked a site this week before reading the solution.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside '3 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know the verdict and the number behind it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart (1 easily, 1 most of the time, 0 sometimes, 1 no) and the bar at 4 of 5 read cleanly, but the count line '2 not counted: a guess · 1 easily · 1 most of the time' runs the for-split into the not-counted reason, so I had to read it twice to see that the two guesses are Marcus and Luis.
screens.why_b3: The condition is mine (talk into their phone over the noise on site), but the belief drops 'on commercial jobs', and the question asks about their 'last daily log' when my occasion is the site walk, where the noise actually is; nobody does the log out on the deck.
screens.why_b4: 'Ray's no is the one to ask about' is a concrete lead, but it doesn't say the plain next step, which is to get two more supers counted, and the closing quote about subs and wind is about the schedule, not about talking over noise.
screens.why_b5: It honestly says 3 is too few and nothing is settled, but asking about 'your last daily log', a trailer moment, makes the noise answers softer than they look, and putting an off-topic quote under Compatibility suggests a theme the answers don't carry.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 2 of 3 counted could talk over the noise on their last site walk, Ray couldn't, and 2 more answers are needed; ask Ray what drowned him out.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its number, 3 counted with 5 needed, and the So line repeats it.
screens.why_b2: Better 2 against Same 1 over 3 counted reads quickly, but the strip's 'your bar 4 of 5' with its marker at 4 sits next to a 1-in-3 rule and '5 needed', and I had to stop and work out which bar is which.
screens.why_b3: The belief line carries both my benefits, hours back and action items to the crew the same day, but the bar line only says 'hours back at the end of the day', and the question asks about any last daily log rather than the one that went wrong.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me to get two more superintendents counted, or that Denise's no-difference shows the log is not her pain.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the guesses are set apart, and 2 of 3 is called a lean, not a call, so nothing claims more than the five answers carry.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 2 of 3 counted said a lot better and 1 said no difference, which is right at your 1-in-3 limit; get 2 more superintendents counted, and note the one who saw no difference already finishes her log on site.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 3 counted against 5 needed, and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count 2 for and 1 against over the 5 who answered, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with its marker at 4 does not obviously match 'no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no', so I had to look twice to see where my bar sits.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Adoption friction and carries my own effort, naming who owns each item as I film, in my words.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me to get two more supers counted, or that both yeses hinge on the naming not slowing the walk, which is the design constraint I'd act on.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the two guesses are shown as not counted, and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than 3 people can carry, though '2 on a condition' sits oddly inside the not-counted list.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 2 of 3 would do it, but only if it keeps the walk moving, and 1 probably not; get 2 more supers counted, and make naming the owner cost no time on the walk.

screens.why_b1: Both boxes open on 'Too few to call' with '3 counted · 5 needed to call it' right beside it, so I know there is no verdict yet and the count that decides it.
screens.why_b3: Both lines are mine as I last checked them: talking into the phone over site noise, and hours back at the end of the day with action items to the crew the same day.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I should get two more answers per line, but the screen never says so, and it doesn't say what the two against-reasons mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: Each box shows the n, says the count is too low, and shows one against with one quote, so nothing claims more than one person said.
screens.why_b6: Denise's log is already done on the tablet before she leaves, and Ray puts the log off till morning when the schedule is slipping; both say the log isn't the pain on the days that matter, which I didn't write in.
screens.instead: Two more answers on each line would let you call it. Meanwhile, the one against on each says the log isn't the bottleneck: subs and schedule are.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check whether my jobs run on Procore or ACC before asking about my daily logs, though the kicker's 'A recent time' doesn't match a question about right now.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are the words we use on every job, and 'the jobs you are running now' is how I'd say it myself.
screens.why3: I know exactly which platform each of my jobs runs on, so I can answer this straight off.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, including a job that runs on both or a mix across jobs, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It only names the platforms my GC already uses, and nothing of anyone's product or plan comes through.
screens.why6: It's one short question with two options, and 'ACC' says fine aloud because supers say it that way.

screens.why1: Right after asking if my jobs run on Procore or ACC, asking about my last week of daily logs is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: These are my own words, but it packs two jobs, uploading photos and typing logs, into one question, so I'd stop and ask whether they mean both and whether 'hours' is per day or for the whole week.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I did with my photos and logs this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No covers it for a gate, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: 'Hours uploading' is how I'd say it myself, and nothing about anybody's product or plan comes through.
screens.why6: It's short, one breath, and ends with 'Yes or no,' so it's easy to answer out loud.
screens.why7: The measure, shape and missing escape are right, but the event is two acts in one, and 'hours' across five working days is something nearly every super logging daily would say Yes to, so a No has little room.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a day when the daily log took you over an hour after your walks? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I spent hours uploading photos and typing logs, showing me the thing meant to fix that is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: It reads clean on one pass, and site walk, crew, assignees and Procore or ACC are all my words, but nobody on a job calls anything a scribe; I'd say an AI note-taker.
screens.why3: I walk the site every day shooting photos and handing out items to subs, so I can picture this on my own walks.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It's shown on purpose as an idea, and the belief about my site walks is plain with nothing else leaking, though it says notes where the first part asked about my daily log.
screens.why6: Short sentences said one after another, and the one list of photos, assignees and due dates is easy to hold; it's long, but it's a card and says well aloud.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an AI note-taker for your site walks. You take short videos and talk over them; it turns them into notes with photos, who's on it and when it's due, texts the crew their items, and sends it all to your daily log in Procore or ACC in one click. The people building it believe it would be used on your site walks.

screens.why1: Right after the Fresco card, it makes sense to ask whether I could even talk into my phone out on a loud site, since that's what the idea depends on.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but the anchor is my last daily log, which I type up in the trailer, while the question asks about talking over the noise on site, so I had to read it twice to see they mean the walk that day.
screens.why3: I walk my site every day with saws, compressors and the crane going, so I know whether I could have talked into my phone out there.
screens.why4: Easily, most of the time, only sometimes and no cover how it goes on site, from a quiet slab day to the framers and the pump truck all going, and I can't tell fits as the way out.
screens.why5: The scribe and site walk videos appear only on the idea card, where I'm told to imagine it, and the question itself is in my own words about my phone and the noise.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold in my head, and the escape is said last.
screens.why7: It's an ability row with the four ability answers in order and I can't tell set apart, it splits supers who can and can't talk over the noise so the belief could hold or fail, and it tests the step the idea rests on, though the card's own example anchors on the site walk rather than the daily log.
screens.instead: Think of your last site walk. Could you have talked into your phone over the noise? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the talk-into-your-phone question, asking whether Fresco would have made my daily log better is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: I get it on first hearing, but nobody on my site says 'keep an accurate record of the day's work', and 'scribe' isn't a word we use; I'd just say 'doing the daily log'.
screens.why3: I write a daily log every day, so I can say from my own last one whether this would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse covers it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' fits as the out.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was shown, but the moment drifted from the founder's pain (hours uploading photos and typing logs) to just any daily log.
screens.why6: The four options say fine as a list, but the opening sentence is long and stiff ('the last daily log when you had to keep an accurate record of the day's work on site'), so you'd have to hold the whole thing to get to the question.
screens.why7: The four fixed options in order with 'I can't tell' apart are right, but the occasion is the routine daily log, not the hard case the study already holds (the day I spent hours uploading photos and typing the log), so a super whose last log went fine just says no difference.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent day you spent hours uploading photos and typing the daily log. Would Fresco, an AI tool for site walks, have helped you get the daily log done better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking whether it would beat my current way of doing daily logs, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually change how I walk to use it.
screens.why2: I'd get it on a second listen, but 'who owns each item' isn't how I talk on a walk; I'd say which sub is responsible for each issue.
screens.why3: I walk the site every day calling out problems, so I know whether I'd stop and name the trade on each one.
screens.why4: Yes, a real condition, probably not, no and can't tell cover it, and 'only if it keeps the walk moving' is exactly my catch.
screens.why5: 'Owns each item' sounds like the software's own vocabulary rather than mine, a small drift toward the product's terms.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options and the escape said last; easy to hold heard once.
screens.why7: It's a new habit I'd take on myself during the walk, the conditional yes is my own specific condition, and two options count for and two against with I can't tell apart.
screens.instead: To use Fresco, you'd say which sub is responsible for each issue as you film. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it keeps the walk moving · Probably not · No · I can't tell
